claim: The conclusion that screening would detect no more than half of infected travellers in a growing epidemic is consistent with recent studies that have compared country-specific air travel volumes with detected case counts to estimate that roughly two thirds of imported cases remain undetected.
source: Our conclusion that screening would detect no more than half of infected travellers in a growing epidemic is consistent with recent studies that have compared country-specific air travel volumes with detected case counts to estimate that roughly two thirds of imported cases remain undetected (Niehus et al., 2020; Bhatia et al., 2020).
evidence: Comparison of model results with independent empirical estimates

claim: The finding that the majority of cases missed by screening are fundamentally undetectable is consistent with observed outcomes so far.
source: Furthermore, the finding that the majority of cases missed by screening are fundamentally undetectable is consistent with observed outcomes so far.
evidence: Comparison of model results with empirical observations

claim: Analyzing a line list of 290 cases imported into various countries, symptom onset occurred after the date of inbound travel for 72% (75/104) of cases for whom both dates were available.
source: Analyzing a line list of 290 cases imported into various countries (Dorigatti et al., 2020), we found that symptom onset occurred after the date of inbound travel for 72% (75/104) of cases for whom both dates were available
evidence: Analysis of empirical data from line list

claim: Among imported cases with known dates, a further 14% (15/104) had symptom onset on the date of travel.
source: and a further 14% (15/104) had symptom onset on the date of travel.
evidence: Analysis of empirical data from line list

claim: Among passengers of repatriation flights or quarantined on a cruise ship off the coast of Japan, numerous cases have been undetectable in symptom screening, but have still tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 by PCR.
source: Even among passengers of repatriation flights, or quarantined on a cruise ship off the coast of Japan (who are all demonstrably at high risk), numerous cases have been undetectable in symptom screening, but have still tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 by PCR (Dorigatti et al., 2020; Hoehl et al., 2020; Japan Ministry of Health, Labor and Welfare, 2020; Nishiura et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to reports of asymptomatic PCR-positive cases

claim: The onset of viral shedding prior to the onset of symptoms, or in cases that remain asymptomatic, is a classic factor that makes infectious disease outbreaks difficult to control.
source: The onset of viral shedding prior to the onset of symptoms, or in cases that remain asymptomatic, is a classic factor that makes infectious disease outbreaks difficult to control (Fraser et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fraser et al., 2004 on outbreak control challenges

claim: The true fraction of subclinical cases (those who lack fever or cough at symptom onset) remains a crucial unknown, and strongly impacts screening effectiveness.
source: Our results emphasize that the true fraction of subclinical cases (those who lack fever or cough at symptom onset) remains a crucial unknown, and strongly impacts screening effectiveness.
evidence: Summary of model results and key uncertainties

claim: Reviewing data from active surveillance of passengers on cruise ships or repatriation flights, up to half of cases show no detectable symptoms at the time of diagnosis.
source: Reviewing data from active surveillance of passengers on cruise ships or repatriation flights, we estimate that up to half of cases show no detectable symptoms at the time of diagnosis.
evidence: Analysis of data from active surveillance contexts

claim: The fraction of subclinical cases may vary across age groups.
source: To complicate matters further, the fraction of subclinical cases may vary across age groups.
evidence: Speculation based on observed age distribution of cases

claim: Children and young adults have been conspicuously underrepresented in very large clinical data sets.
source: Children and young adults have been conspicuously underrepresented, even in very large clinical data sets (Chen et al., 2020; The Novel Coronavirus Pneumonia Emergency Response Epidemiology Team, 2020; Huang et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple clinical and epidemiological studies

claim: Only 2.1% of the first 44,672 confirmed COVID-19 cases were observed in children under 20 years of age.
source: Only 2.1% of the first 44,672 confirmed cases were observed in children under 20 years of age (The Novel Coronavirus Pneumonia Emergency Response Epidemiology Team, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to epidemiological report with specific data

claim: The possibility cannot be ruled out that large numbers of subclinical cases are occurring in young people.
source: The possibility cannot be ruled out that large numbers of subclinical cases are occurring in young people.
evidence: Speculation based on observed age distribution

claim: If an age-by-severity interaction does indeed exist, then the mean age of travellers should be taken into account when estimating screening effectiveness.
source: If an age-by-severity interaction does indeed exist, then the mean age of travellers should be taken into account when estimating screening effectiveness.
evidence: Recommendation based on potential age-severity relationship

claim: Parameter values for COVID-19 may be affected by bias or censoring, particularly in the early stages of an outbreak when most cases have been recently infected, and when severe or hospitalized cases are overrepresented in the available data.
source: Parameter values for COVID-19 may be affected by bias or censoring, particularly in the early stages of an outbreak when most cases have been recently infected, and when severe or hospitalized cases are overrepresented in the available data.
evidence: Acknowledgment of potential biases in early outbreak data

claim: The tail of the incubation period distribution is difficult to characterize with precision using limited or biased data.
source: In particular, the tail of the incubation period distribution is difficult to characterize with precision using limited or biased data.
evidence: Statement about statistical challenges with limited data

claim: There are informal reports of people taking antipyretics to beat fever screening.
source: However, there are informal reports of people taking antipyretics to beat fever screening (Mahbubani, 2020), which would further reduce the effectiveness of these methods.
evidence: Supported by citation to news report

claim: Taking antipyretics to beat fever screening would further reduce the effectiveness of screening methods.
source: However, there are informal reports of people taking antipyretics to beat fever screening (Mahbubani, 2020), which would further reduce the effectiveness of these methods.
evidence: Logical inference from evasion behavior

claim: With travel restrictions in place, individuals may take alternative routes (e.g. road rather than air), which would in effect circumvent departure and/or arrival screening as a control measure.
source: With travel restrictions in place, individuals may also take alternative routes (e.g. road rather than air), which would in effect circumvent departure and/or arrival screening as a control measure.
evidence: Speculation about potential evasion strategies

claim: The quantitative findings may overestimate screening effectiveness if many travellers evade screening.
source: Our quantitative findings may overestimate screening effectiveness if many travellers evade screening.
evidence: Acknowledgment of model limitation

claim: If the infection is not yet present in a region, then arrival screening could delay the introduction of cases.
source: If the infection is not yet present in a region, then arrival screening could delay the introduction of cases
evidence: Inference about potential benefit of screening

claim: Consistent with previous analyses, delays from arrival screening would be minimal.
source: but consistent with previous analyses, (Cowling et al., 2010), our results indicate such delays would be minimal.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous analysis and current model results

claim: For every case detected by travel screening, one or more infected travellers were not caught, and must be found and isolated by other means.
source: Our findings indicate that for every case detected by travel screening, one or more infected travellers were not caught, and must be found and isolated by other means.
evidence: Inference from model results on screening effectiveness

claim: Even with high R0 and no control measures in place, a single case importation is not guaranteed to start a sustained chain of transmission.
source: We note that even with high R0 and no control measures in place, a single case importation is not guaranteed to start a sustained chain of transmission (Kucharski et al., 2020; Lloyd-Smith et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on transmission dynamics

claim: COVID-19 exhibits a tendency toward superspreading events.
source: This is particularly true for infections that exhibit a tendency toward superspreading events, as increasingly reported for COVID-19
evidence: Reference to emerging evidence about COVID-19 transmission patterns

claim: Outbreaks triggered by superspreading are explosive when they do occur.
source: but the flipside is that outbreaks triggered by superspreading are explosive when they do occur (Lloyd-Smith et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lloyd-Smith et al., 2005 on superspreading dynamics

claim: Official recommendations emphasize that screening is an opportunity for 'risk communication' in which travellers can be instructed how to proceed responsibly if symptoms develop at the destination.
source: Official recommendations emphasize that screening is an opportunity for 'risk communication' in which travellers can be instructed how to proceed responsibly if symptoms develop at the destination (World Health Organization, 2020d).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO guidance

claim: Alongside increased general surveillance/alertness in healthcare settings, risk communication measures could help reduce the risk of local transmission and superspreading, but their quantitative effectiveness is unknown.
source: Alongside increased general surveillance/alertness in healthcare settings, such measures could help reduce the risk of local transmission and superspreading, but their quantitative effectiveness is unknown.
evidence: Speculation about potential benefits with acknowledgment of uncertainty

claim: Once limited local transmission has begun, arrival screening could still have merit as a means to restrict the number of parallel chains of transmission present in a country.
source: Once limited local transmission has begun, arrival screening could still have merit as a means to restrict the number of parallel chains of transmission present in a country.
evidence: Inference about potential benefit in specific epidemiological context

claim: Once there is generalized spread which has outpaced contact tracing, departure screening to prevent export of cases to new areas will be more valuable than arrival screening to identify additional incoming cases.
source: Once there is generalized spread which has outpaced contact tracing, departure screening to prevent export of cases to new areas will be more valuable than arrival screening to identify additional incoming cases.
evidence: Inference about relative value of screening strategies in different epidemic phases

claim: Screening should not be viewed as a definitive barrier to case importation, but used alongside on-the-ground response strategies that help reduce the probability that any single imported case spreads to cause a self-sustaining local epidemic.
source: Altogether, screening should not be viewed as a definitive barrier to case importation, but used alongside on-the-ground response strategies that help reduce the probability that any single imported case spreads to cause a self-sustaining local epidemic.
evidence: Recommendation based on model results and epidemiological reasoning

claim: The cost-benefit tradeoff for any screening policy should be assessed in light of past experiences, where few or no infected travellers have been detected by such programs.
source: The cost-benefit tradeoff for any screening policy should be assessed in light of past experiences, where few or no infected travellers have been detected by such programs (Gostic et al., 2015).
evidence: Recommendation supported by citation to previous analysis

claim: The majority of screening failures arise from undetectable cases (i.e. those without symptoms or knowledge of their exposure).
source: While our findings indicate that the majority of screening failures arise from undetectable cases (i.e. those without symptoms or knowledge of their exposure)
evidence: Summary of model results

claim: With improved efficiency of thermal scanners or other symptom detection technology, we would expect a smaller difference between the effectiveness of arrival-only screening and combined departure and arrival screening.
source: With improved efficiency of thermal scanners or other symptom detection technology, we would expect a smaller difference between the effectiveness of arrival-only screening and combined departure and arrival screening in our analysis.
evidence: Inference about impact of improved technology on screening outcomes

claim: The benefits of redundant screening could be gained in a single-site screening program by simply having two successive fever-screening stations that travellers pass through (or taking multiple measurements of each traveller at a single station).
source: Alternatively, the benefits of redundant screening (noted above for programs with departure and arrival screens) could be gained in a single-site screening program by simply having two successive fever-screening stations that travellers pass through (or taking multiple measurements of each traveller at a single station).
evidence: Recommendation based on model results about redundancy benefits

claim: As risk factors become better known, questionnaires could be refined to identify more potential cases.
source: As risk factors become better known, questionnaires could be refined to identify more potential cases.
evidence: Recommendation for future improvement

claim: Less stringent definition of high exposure risk (e.g. contact with anyone with respiratory symptoms) would be more sensitive, but at the expense of large numbers of false positives detained, especially during influenza season.
source: Alternatively, less stringent definition of high exposure risk (e.g. contact with anyone with respiratory symptoms) would be more sensitive, but at the expense of large numbers of false positives detained, especially during influenza season.
evidence: Inference about tradeoffs in screening criteria

claim: The availability of rapid PCR tests would be beneficial for case identification at arrival.
source: The availability of rapid PCR tests would also be beneficial for case identification at arrival
evidence: Inference about potential improvement to screening

claim: Rapid PCR tests would help address concerns with false-positive detections by screening.
source: and would help address concerns with false-positive detections by screening.
evidence: Inference about benefit of confirmatory testing

claim: At least one PCR test for SARS-CoV-2 claimed to take less than an hour has been announced.
source: at least one PCR test for SARS-CoV-2 claimed to take less than an hour has already been announced (Biomeme, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Biomeme announcement

claim: Rapid PCR testing measures could prove highly expensive if implemented at scale.
source: However, such measures could prove highly expensive if implemented at scale.
evidence: Inference about resource implications

claim: There is scope for new tools to improve the ongoing tracking of travellers who pass through screening, such as smartphone-based self-reporting of temperature or symptoms in incoming cases.
source: There is also scope for new tools to improve the ongoing tracking of travellers who pass through screening, such as smartphone-based self-reporting of temperature or symptoms in incoming cases (Dorigatti et al., 2020).
evidence: Suggestion for improvement with citation to example

claim: Smartphone or diary-based surveillance would be cheaper and more scalable than intense, on-the-ground follow-up, but is likely to be limited by user adherence.
source: Smartphone or diary-based surveillance would be cheaper and more scalable than intense, on-the-ground follow-up, but is likely to be limited by user adherence.
evidence: Inference about tradeoffs of digital surveillance approaches

claim: Respiratory viruses are difficult to detect by symptom and risk screening programs, particularly if a substantial fraction of infected people show mild or indistinct symptoms, if incubation periods are long, and if transmission is possible before the onset of symptoms.
source: Our analysis underscores the reality that respiratory viruses are difficult to detect by symptom and risk screening programs, particularly if a substantial fraction of infected people show mild or indistinct symptoms, if incubation periods are long, and if transmission is possible before the onset of symptoms.
evidence: Summary of key findings with general principle

claim: In any situation where there is widespread epidemic transmission in source populations from which travellers are drawn, travel screening programs can slow (marginally) but not stop the importation of infected cases.
source: However, we present a robust qualitative finding: in any situation where there is widespread epidemic transmission in source populations from which travellers are drawn, travel screening programs can slow (marginally) but not stop the importation of infected cases.
evidence: Summary of key finding from model results

claim: Screening programs implemented in other settings will face the same challenges as travel screening.
source: Screening programs implemented in other settings will face the same challenges.
evidence: Generalization of findings to other screening contexts

claim: A delay-adjusted estimate indicates 34.6% of infections are asymptomatic.
source: Since resubmission, a new delay-adjusted estimate indicates that 34.6% of infections are asymptomatic (Mizumoto et al., 2020), intermediate between our middle and worst-case scenarios.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mizumoto et al., 2020 study

claim: The 34.6% asymptomatic infection estimate is intermediate between the middle and worst-case scenarios used in the analysis.
source: Since resubmission, a new delay-adjusted estimate indicates that 34.6% of infections are asymptomatic (Mizumoto et al., 2020), intermediate between our middle and worst-case scenarios.
evidence: Comparison of new estimate with model scenarios
